summary: Adds a CalDAV extension that lets attachments for iCalendar data be stored and managed on the server. It documents code already deployed by multiple vendors, and was published as informational because it departs from several HTTP best practices.

plainLanguage.summary: This lets calendar programs keep files attached to events on the server, as many already did. It was written to record existing practice.

questions: how to attach files to calendar events
subtitle: Storing and managing calendar event attachments on the server

tldr.problem: Calendar applications often need to attach files like meeting agendas to events, but iCalendar's inline attachment storage requires re-uploading the entire file whenever the event changes, and URL-based attachments raise discovery and access control issues.
tldr.mechanism: This extension lets clients upload attachments separately to the server via HTTP POST and reference them with special parameters, while the server manages access control and generates unique identifiers.
tldr.outcome: Attachments are stored once and reused across multiple events, with the server handling access control. Published as Informational because it departs from HTTP best practices, but widely deployed.

today: RFC 8607 is an Informational specification documenting widely deployed practice. It has not been obsoleted and remains in use by major calendar vendors for server-side attachment management in CalDAV implementations.

sections.title: Calendar Attachments
sections.content:
Calendar applications frequently need to attach files to events, such as meeting agendas, presentations, or travel documents. iCalendar, the standard format for calendar data, provides an ATTACH property for this purpose. However, it has two major problems: embedding attachment data directly in the calendar requires re-uploading the entire file on every event change, and storing only a URL gives no standard way to discover where files are kept or ensure attendees can access them.

This specification solves both problems by having the server manage attachments separately from the calendar data. The client uploads files to the server via HTTP POST, the server stores them and generates unique identifiers, and the calendar data simply includes a URL and metadata parameters pointing to the stored file.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of pasting the same photo into every letter you send, you can upload it to a mailroom, get a sticker with its location, and just stick that on your letters. The mailroom keeps copies and controls who can peek inside.

sections.title: Managing Attachments
sections.content:
Clients perform four operations on attachments: adding, updating, removing, and retrieving them. All of these except retrieval use POST requests to the calendar object resource with query parameters specifying the action and which recurrence instances to target.

To add an attachment, the client sends a POST request with action=attachment-add and the file data in the request body. The server stores the file, generates a unique MANAGED-ID, adds an ATTACH property to the calendar data, and returns the managed ID in a Cal-Managed-ID response header. To update an existing attachment, the client uses action=attachment-update with the managed ID to replace the file; the server changes the MANAGED-ID value so other clients can detect the update. To remove an attachment, the client sends action=attachment-remove with the managed ID; the server deletes the attachment property and can clean up the file if no other calendar data references it. Retrieving attachments is just a normal HTTP GET on the attachment URI stored in the calendar data.

All three operations support the rid parameter to target specific recurrence instances (like one occurrence of a recurring event), or omit it to affect all instances.
sections.plainLanguage: You can tell the mailroom to add a new document, replace an old one, or stop keeping one. You name which letter or which specific date it applies to. Getting your document back is just asking the mailroom for it by the location code.

sections.title: iCalendar Extensions
sections.content:
CalDAV managed attachments introduce three new parameters for the ATTACH property in iCalendar data:

MANAGED-ID is a unique identifier generated by the server that permanently identifies a particular managed attachment within that server. It lets clients and other services recognize the same attachment across calendar updates.

FILENAME tells the client what filename to use when storing the attachment locally. For example, ATTACH;FILENAME=agenda.html:https://... suggests the file should be saved as agenda.html.

SIZE specifies the attachment size in octets (bytes), allowing clients to know download sizes without fetching the entire file. Defined as text rather than a number to support arbitrarily large files.

Together with existing iCalendar parameters like FMTTYPE (the media type), these parameters let the server provide clients with enough information to efficiently manage and display attachments.
sections.plainLanguage: When the mailroom stores something, it writes down: what it is (a PDF), how big it is (100 KB), and what to call it (budget.pdf). That way, someone reading your letter knows what they're getting before asking for it.

sections.title: Security and Access Control
sections.content:
The specification defines several security requirements. Only event organizers may add, update, or remove managed attachments; attendees cannot. Users cannot reuse a managed attachment (by its ID) unless they created it. Access to attachment files must be restricted to those who can access the calendar event itself, either directly or as an invited attendee.

Servers must validate attachment size limits and the total number of attachments per calendar object. They should check attachments for malicious content and may automatically remove them if threats are detected. Since attachments are propagated to attendees via scheduling messages, servers must notify attendees when attachments change.

The specification also advises servers to be aware of potential abuse: clients could attack storage by uploading extremely large attachments, or attack processing time by repeatedly modifying recurring events with many overrides.
sections.plainLanguage: Only the person who organized the meeting can add or remove documents. Everyone invited to the meeting can see them, but only them. The mailroom checks that documents aren't dangerous and aren't taking up too much space.

sections.title: Deployment and Interoperability
sections.content:
The server advertises support for managed attachments by including calendar-managed-attachments as a token in the DAV response header from an OPTIONS request on a calendar home collection. Some servers may not support per-recurrence-instance attachments (adding different attachments to different occurrences of a recurring event); in that case they advertise calendar-managed-attachments-no-recurrence so clients know not to attempt such operations.

Servers expose three WebDAV properties to clients: a managed-attachments-server-URL property may specify an alternate base URI for retrieving attachments, a max-attachment-size property sets the maximum file size in octets, and a max-attachments-per-resource property limits how many attachments can be associated with a single calendar event. When exporting or importing calendar data, clients should remove all MANAGED-ID parameters to avoid conflicts on the destination server.
sections.plainLanguage: The calendar server tells clients: yes, I can handle managed attachments, here is where to fetch them from, and I allow files up to 100 MB each, with at most 20 files per event. When you move events to another server, don't try to reuse the old storage locations.
